titulo: Could You Survive a Year as a Medieval Peasant? (1348)
descripcion:
You wake up on March 25th, 1348 — New Year's Day in medieval England — as Stan, an unfree peasant on a manor in Dorset. Your mission: survive one year. You'll deal with a lord who owns your labor, the tithe, endless pottage, the harvest… and the Black Death, which lands in England that very summer.

A stickman history story with real facts and sources.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Waking Up in 1348
0:34 Your New Home
1:07 Who Owns You?
2:31 Spring: Mud, Oxen and Porridge
4:01 Wait… Were They Really That Dirty?
4:30 Summer: Something Is Coming
5:58 Autumn: The Harvest Nobody Can Bring In
6:51 Winter: Salt, Smoke and Christmas
7:24 Did You Survive?

REAL HISTORY IN THIS VIDEO
• England's civil/legal year began on 25 March until 1752
• The Black Death reached England in 1348
• Peasant houses were timber-framed with wattle-and-daub walls and thatched roofs
• Most peasant houses had an open central hearth and no chimney
• In some regions peasants lived in longhouses shared with livestock
• Villeins were unfree tenants legally bound to their lord's manor
• Villeins typically owed 'week-work' on the lord's demesne, often 2-3 days per week
• The lord's demesne was farmed using villeins' labor services
• The reeve was a villager chosen to oversee work on the manor
• Merchet was a fine paid to the lord when an unfree woman married
• Heriot: on a tenant's death the lord took the best beast
• Tenants were often obliged to use the lord's mill and pay a toll (multure) in grain

Stan's story is a dramatization; the historical facts are real, simplified for the video, and sourced below. Numbers are estimates — historians argue about the details, and that's part of the fun.

SOURCES & FURTHER READING

• H. S. Bennett, Life on the English Manor (Cambridge, 1937)
• Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (2008)
• Glanvill, Treatise on the Laws of England (c. 1188)
• William Chester Jordan, The Great Famine (Princeton, 1996)
• Katherine Harvey, The Fires of Lust / Smithsonian, 'Medieval people did bathe'
• CDC, 'Plague: symptoms and transmission'
• Ole J. Benedictow, The Black Death 1346-1353 (Boydell, 2004)
• British Library, 'Medieval medicine and the plague doctor'
• Museum of London Archaeology
• Ordinance of Labourers (1349) & Statute of Labourers (1351), UK Parliament

1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:04,458
It's the morning of March twenty-fifth,
1348, and you just woke up on a pile

2
00:00:04,478 --> 00:00:05,247
of straw.

3
00:00:05,267 --> 00:00:06,529
Congratulations.

4
00:00:06,549 --> 00:00:10,383
You are a medieval peasant, and your
mission is simple: survive one year.

5
00:00:10,403 --> 00:00:11,732
Oh, and happy New Year!

6
00:00:11,752 --> 00:00:15,280
In medieval England, the year officially
started on March twenty-fifth.

7
00:00:15,300 --> 00:00:17,392
Now, I'm going to be honest with you.

8
00:00:17,412 --> 00:00:19,147
Of all the years you could have picked…

9
00:00:19,167 --> 00:00:23,555
Here's how this works: every chapter,
Stan's survival odds go up or down,

10
00:00:23,575 --> 00:00:25,480
depending on what life throws at him.

11
00:00:25,500 --> 00:00:26,684
this is the worst one.

12
00:00:26,704 --> 00:00:29,443
By the end of it, a huge part of England
will be dead.

13
00:00:29,463 --> 00:00:33,357
So let's see what it takes to make it
through 1348, one season at a time.

14
00:00:33,377 --> 00:00:34,027
Ready?

15
00:00:34,047 --> 00:00:34,747
Let's go.

16
00:00:34,767 --> 00:00:36,189
Let's start with your house.

17
00:00:36,209 --> 00:00:39,983
It's one room, built from a wooden frame
packed with mud and straw.

18
00:00:40,003 --> 00:00:41,102
There's no chimney.

19
00:00:41,122 --> 00:00:44,708
The fire burns in the middle of the floor,
and the smoke just…

20
00:00:44,728 --> 00:00:45,716
finds its way out.

21
00:00:45,736 --> 00:00:49,285
The floor is packed earth covered in
straw, which is cozy, right up until

22
00:00:49,305 --> 00:00:50,513
you meet the rats.

23
00:00:50,533 --> 00:00:51,625
And you're not alone.

24
00:00:51,645 --> 00:00:54,247
Meet your wife, Maud, and your son, Wat.

25
00:00:54,267 --> 00:00:58,580
Also living with you: a pig, a few
chickens, and, if you're lucky, a cow.

26
00:00:58,600 --> 00:01:02,094
In many longhouses, the animals lived at
one end of the building.

27
00:01:02,114 --> 00:01:04,383
Their body heat kept everyone warm.

28
00:01:04,403 --> 00:01:05,240
The smell?

29
00:01:05,260 --> 00:01:07,647
Let's just say you stop noticing it after
a week.

30
00:01:07,667 --> 00:01:09,259
Here's the first bad news.

31
00:01:09,279 --> 00:01:10,811
You don't really own anything.

32
00:01:10,831 --> 00:01:12,650
Not the land, not the house…

33
00:01:12,670 --> 00:01:14,513
and in a way, not even yourself.

34
00:01:14,533 --> 00:01:15,847
Because this guy does.

35
00:01:15,867 --> 00:01:17,951
You're a villein, an unfree peasant.

36
00:01:17,971 --> 00:01:20,747
You're bound to Sir Hugh's manor, and you
can't just leave.

37
00:01:20,767 --> 00:01:23,661
In exchange for your strips of land, you
owe him work.

38
00:01:23,681 --> 00:01:26,547
Often two or three days a week, every
week.

39
00:01:26,567 --> 00:01:30,056
That's free labor on his fields, called
the demesne, while your own crops

40
00:01:30,076 --> 00:01:30,647
wait.

41
00:01:30,667 --> 00:01:34,726
Making sure you actually show up is the
reeve, a fellow peasant with a clipboard

42
00:01:34,746 --> 00:01:35,513
energy.

43
00:01:35,533 --> 00:01:36,525
And the fees.

44
00:01:36,545 --> 00:01:37,597
Oh, the fees.

45
00:01:37,617 --> 00:01:38,969
Want your daughter to marry?

46
00:01:38,989 --> 00:01:41,080
Pay the lord a fine, called merchet.

47
00:01:41,100 --> 00:01:43,256
When you die, he takes your best animal.

48
00:01:43,276 --> 00:01:44,747
That one is called heriot.

49
00:01:44,767 --> 00:01:45,767
Need flour?

50
00:01:45,787 --> 00:01:48,813
You must grind your grain at his mill, and
he keeps a cut of it.

51
00:01:48,833 --> 00:01:52,271
And then there's the Church, which takes a
tithe: one tenth of everything

52
00:01:52,291 --> 00:01:53,216
you produce.

53
00:01:53,236 --> 00:01:56,612
Break the rules, and you'll end up in the
manor court, where your own neighbors

54
00:01:56,632 --> 00:01:58,083
help decide your fine.

55
00:01:58,103 --> 00:01:59,370
Typical crimes?

56
00:01:59,390 --> 00:02:03,913
Letting your pig wander into the lord's
crops, or brewing ale that's too weak.

57
00:02:03,933 --> 00:02:07,477
And if someone shouts that a crime has
happened, everyone must drop what they're

58
00:02:07,497 --> 00:02:09,380
doing and chase the culprit.

59
00:02:09,400 --> 00:02:12,980
Add it all up, and a big share of your
work never feeds your own family.

60
00:02:13,000 --> 00:02:15,442
Some of your rent isn't even paid in
money.

61
00:02:15,462 --> 00:02:18,513
It's paid in hens at Christmas and eggs at
Easter.

62
00:02:18,533 --> 00:02:19,893
Your one legal escape?

63
00:02:19,913 --> 00:02:23,796
Run to a chartered town and live there for
a year and a day without being

64
00:02:23,816 --> 00:02:24,535
caught.

65
00:02:24,555 --> 00:02:25,380
Then you're free.

66
00:02:25,400 --> 00:02:27,274
Still, it's not all misery.

67
00:02:27,294 --> 00:02:30,980
Sundays and dozens of holy days are days
off from field work.

68
00:02:31,000 --> 00:02:32,964
It's spring, so it's time to plough.

69
00:02:32,984 --> 00:02:36,880
Your village farms huge open fields
divided into long strips.

70
00:02:36,900 --> 00:02:40,620
Your strips are scattered all over, so the
good soil and the bad soil get

71
00:02:40,640 --> 00:02:41,613
shared around.

72
00:02:41,633 --> 00:02:45,890
A typical villein family might hold around
thirty acres, but plenty of families

73
00:02:45,910 --> 00:02:47,080
had much less.

74
00:02:47,100 --> 00:02:51,352
Nobody owns enough oxen to pull a heavy
plough alone, so neighbors share their

75
00:02:51,372 --> 00:02:52,180
animals.

76
00:02:52,200 --> 00:02:56,547
Each year, one big field rests, called
fallow, so the soil can recover.

77
00:02:56,567 --> 00:02:59,209
You work from sunrise until the light is
gone.

78
00:02:59,229 --> 00:03:00,416
So, what's for lunch?

79
00:03:00,436 --> 00:03:01,175
Pottage.

80
00:03:01,195 --> 00:03:05,847
A thick stew of grains, peas, beans and
whatever vegetables are growing.

81
00:03:05,867 --> 00:03:06,709
Tomorrow?

82
00:03:06,729 --> 00:03:07,471
Pottage.

83
00:03:07,491 --> 00:03:08,459
The day after?

84
00:03:08,479 --> 00:03:09,213
You guessed it.

85
00:03:09,233 --> 00:03:14,009
Add dark bread made from rye or barley,
and a little cheese, eggs, or bacon

86
00:03:14,029 --> 00:03:15,113
when you can get them.

87
00:03:15,133 --> 00:03:16,063
And to drink?

88
00:03:16,083 --> 00:03:16,665
Ale.

89
00:03:16,685 --> 00:03:17,417
Lots of it.

90
00:03:17,437 --> 00:03:20,816
Weak, cloudy ale was a daily food, not a
party drink.

91
00:03:20,836 --> 00:03:22,475
People did drink water too.

92
00:03:22,495 --> 00:03:25,313
But ale was safer, tastier, and it filled
you up.

93
00:03:25,333 --> 00:03:27,265
Maud works just as hard as you.

94
00:03:27,285 --> 00:03:32,013
She brews, spins wool, makes cheese, keeps
the animals, and helps in the fields.

95
00:03:32,033 --> 00:03:32,823
And Wat?

96
00:03:32,843 --> 00:03:37,171
At seven, he's already working: collecting
firewood, minding geese, and scaring

97
00:03:37,191 --> 00:03:38,680
birds off the seeds.

98
00:03:38,700 --> 00:03:42,440
Your clothes are simple: a wool tunic,
linen underneath, and a hood.

99
00:03:42,460 --> 00:03:44,113
You own maybe two outfits.

100
00:03:44,133 --> 00:03:47,731
And then there's the hungry gap: late
spring, when last year's food is running

101
00:03:47,751 --> 00:03:50,077
out, and the new crops aren't ready yet.

102
00:03:50,097 --> 00:03:54,859
Your parents remember the Great Famine of
1315 to 1317.

103
00:03:54,879 --> 00:03:57,450
Years of rain, rotting crops, and hunger.

104
00:03:57,470 --> 00:04:01,250
So every spring, you plant, you pray, and
you hope the weather behaves.

105
00:04:01,270 --> 00:04:02,289
Quick myth check.

106
00:04:02,309 --> 00:04:05,201
You've probably heard that medieval people
never washed.

107
00:04:05,221 --> 00:04:06,013
Not true.

108
00:04:06,033 --> 00:04:09,967
Washing your hands and face every morning
was normal, and towns had public

109
00:04:09,987 --> 00:04:11,947
bathhouses, called stews.

110
00:04:11,967 --> 00:04:14,397
And the idea that everyone died at thirty?

111
00:04:14,417 --> 00:04:16,780
That average is dragged down by children.

112
00:04:16,800 --> 00:04:20,522
Sadly, around one in three children didn't
reach adulthood.

113
00:04:20,542 --> 00:04:23,877
But if you did, reaching your fifties or
sixties was normal.

114
00:04:23,897 --> 00:04:28,203
So, rule one of surviving 1348: get past
childhood.

115
00:04:28,223 --> 00:04:30,050
Good news: you already did.

116
00:04:30,070 --> 00:04:30,729
Summer.

117
00:04:30,749 --> 00:04:34,150
The crops are growing, the hay needs
cutting, and the village is busy.

118
00:04:34,170 --> 00:04:37,980
But around the end of June, a ship docks
at Melcombe, a port in Dorset.

119
00:04:38,000 --> 00:04:40,838
On board is something nobody can see:
plague.

120
00:04:40,858 --> 00:04:42,913
The Black Death has reached England.

121
00:04:42,933 --> 00:04:46,999
It's caused by a bacterium, Yersinia
pestis, carried by fleas that live on

122
00:04:47,019 --> 00:04:48,613
rats, and on people.

123
00:04:48,633 --> 00:04:51,927
Of course, nobody in 1348 knows that.

124
00:04:51,947 --> 00:04:55,150
Doctors blame bad air, the stars, or God's
anger.

125
00:04:55,170 --> 00:04:58,871
And no, the famous beaked plague doctor
mask wasn't around yet.

126
00:04:58,891 --> 00:05:00,880
That shows up in the sixteen hundreds.

127
00:05:00,900 --> 00:05:03,102
By July the plague is spreading inland.

128
00:05:03,122 --> 00:05:06,580
Village by village, the news arrives
before the disease does.

129
00:05:06,600 --> 00:05:09,644
It reaches Bristol in August, and London
by the autumn.

130
00:05:09,664 --> 00:05:11,916
Wherever people travel, it travels too.

131
00:05:11,936 --> 00:05:16,225
The symptoms are terrifying: fever, and
painful swellings called buboes in

132
00:05:16,245 --> 00:05:17,847
the armpits or groin.

133
00:05:17,867 --> 00:05:20,109
Many of the sick die within a week.

134
00:05:20,129 --> 00:05:21,071
Some recover.

135
00:05:21,091 --> 00:05:22,280
Nobody knows why.

136
00:05:22,300 --> 00:05:25,144
Stan's family stays home, prays, and
waits.

137
00:05:25,164 --> 00:05:27,880
Every cough in the night sounds like a
death sentence.

138
00:05:27,900 --> 00:05:30,114
By autumn, the plague is in your village.

139
00:05:30,134 --> 00:05:31,516
Your neighbor goes first.

140
00:05:31,536 --> 00:05:32,450
Then the priest.

141
00:05:32,470 --> 00:05:33,671
People try everything.

142
00:05:33,691 --> 00:05:37,693
Processions, prayers, bonfires, fleeing to
the countryside.

143
00:05:37,713 --> 00:05:38,847
Nothing seems to work.

144
00:05:38,867 --> 00:05:42,841
Graveyards fill up so fast that new burial
grounds are opened, like the one

145
00:05:42,861 --> 00:05:44,680
at East Smithfield in London.

146
00:05:44,700 --> 00:05:48,934
Across England, somewhere between a third
and a half of the population dies.

147
00:05:48,954 --> 00:05:49,947
Possibly more.

148
00:05:49,967 --> 00:05:51,371
Whole families vanish.

149
00:05:51,391 --> 00:05:53,247
Some villages are simply abandoned.

150
00:05:53,267 --> 00:05:54,179
And Stan?

151
00:05:54,199 --> 00:05:55,339
Stan gets lucky.

152
00:05:55,359 --> 00:05:56,441
Maud and Wat too.

153
00:05:56,461 --> 00:05:58,647
Nobody really knows why some survived.

154
00:05:58,667 --> 00:06:01,651
Now it's harvest time, the most important
weeks of the year.

155
00:06:01,671 --> 00:06:03,147
But half the workers are gone.

156
00:06:03,167 --> 00:06:07,362
Chroniclers describe crops rotting in the
fields and animals wandering with

157
00:06:07,382 --> 00:06:09,147
nobody to look after them.

158
00:06:09,167 --> 00:06:12,293
Which means, for the first time in your
life, you have something the lord

159
00:06:12,313 --> 00:06:13,613
desperately needs.

160
00:06:13,633 --> 00:06:14,425
Your labor.

161
00:06:14,445 --> 00:06:17,916
Workers are suddenly rare, so they start
demanding higher wages.

162
00:06:17,936 --> 00:06:19,315
The government panics.

163
00:06:19,335 --> 00:06:23,880
In 1349, a new law tries to freeze wages
at pre-plague levels.

164
00:06:23,900 --> 00:06:28,002
On many manors, lords also start swapping
your labor services for a simple

165
00:06:28,022 --> 00:06:28,964
money rent.

166
00:06:28,984 --> 00:06:30,813
Fewer days working his fields.

167
00:06:30,833 --> 00:06:32,085
It doesn't really work.

168
00:06:32,105 --> 00:06:35,947
Lords quietly break it themselves, because
otherwise their crops rot.

169
00:06:35,967 --> 00:06:37,569
There's also empty land now.

170
00:06:37,589 --> 00:06:41,436
Holdings whose families died are suddenly
available, and some survivors grab

171
00:06:41,456 --> 00:06:41,947
them.

172
00:06:41,967 --> 00:06:43,221
It's a strange feeling.

173
00:06:43,241 --> 00:06:47,547
The worst year in memory is also the first
time peasants hold some real power.

174
00:06:47,567 --> 00:06:51,125
Before winter, you thresh the grain, store
it, and pay your tithe.

175
00:06:51,145 --> 00:06:51,880
Again.

176
00:06:51,900 --> 00:06:53,352
November is slaughter month.

177
00:06:53,372 --> 00:06:57,180
Animals you can't feed through winter are
killed, and their meat is salted.

178
00:06:57,200 --> 00:06:59,144
Winter is long, dark and cold.

179
00:06:59,164 --> 00:07:01,950
The whole family sleeps close together by
the fire.

180
00:07:01,970 --> 00:07:04,813
But then comes the best part of the year:
Christmas.

181
00:07:04,833 --> 00:07:06,047
Twelve whole days of it.

182
00:07:06,067 --> 00:07:10,161
Work on the lord's land stops, and on many
manors, the lord even provides

183
00:07:10,181 --> 00:07:11,847
a feast for his tenants.

184
00:07:11,867 --> 00:07:14,713
For a few days, there's meat, ale, and
music.

185
00:07:14,733 --> 00:07:17,283
And then, slowly, the light returns.

186
00:07:17,303 --> 00:07:21,584
The rest of winter is quiet work indoors:
mending tools, spinning, telling

187
00:07:21,604 --> 00:07:24,113
stories by the fire, and waiting for
spring.

188
00:07:24,133 --> 00:07:26,407
March twenty-fourth, 1349.

189
00:07:26,427 --> 00:07:27,789
The last day of your year.

190
00:07:27,809 --> 00:07:28,913
Let's check the score.

191
00:07:28,933 --> 00:07:33,031
You survived the work, the fees, the
pottage, the winter, and the deadliest

192
00:07:33,051 --> 00:07:35,147
pandemic in European history.

193
00:07:35,167 --> 00:07:39,055
Final tally: a penny or two a day before
the plague, and up to three pennies

194
00:07:39,075 --> 00:07:39,815
after.

195
00:07:39,835 --> 00:07:42,007
Around three hundred bowls of pottage.

196
00:07:42,027 --> 00:07:43,713
And one very lucky family.

197
00:07:43,733 --> 00:07:44,885
And here's the twist.

198
00:07:44,905 --> 00:07:46,697
Your world is about to change.

199
00:07:46,717 --> 00:07:49,843
With so few workers left, peasants start
to push back.

200
00:07:49,863 --> 00:07:53,077
In 1381, they rise up in the Peasants'
Revolt.

201
00:07:53,097 --> 00:07:56,743
Within a few generations, serfdom in
England fades away.

202
00:07:56,763 --> 00:07:59,823
So, would you have survived 1348?

203
00:07:59,843 --> 00:08:01,980
And what's the first modern thing you'd
miss?

204
00:08:02,000 --> 00:08:03,292
Tell me in the comments.

205
00:08:03,312 --> 00:08:06,166
And if you enjoyed surviving with Stan,
subscribe.

206
00:08:06,186 --> 00:08:08,728
Next time, we go somewhere even worse.
